title: The Gang Wins the Big Game

jokes.text: Mac corrects Charlie's word 'stupidstition' but his correction reveals he understands it's a stupid superstition — which is actually Charlie's point in disguise
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie the word is 'superstition,' not 'stupidstition,' positioning himself as the smart one
jokes.punchline: 'I'm saying your Green Man suit is a stupid superstition' — Mac's correction accidentally proves Charlie's portmanteau was perfect
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie wordplay that actually contains more logic than the correction. Mac's self-important grammar lesson undermines itself perfectly. Strong character integration — this is exactly how these two interact. The layered joke (Charlie's dumb word is smarter than Mac realizes) gives it rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The word is "superstition," not "stupidstition."

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I know what the word is, Charlie. I'm saying your Green Man suit is a stupid superstition.

jokes.text: Mac claims he's not a Cowboys fan, he's a 'Tony Romo fan,' and since Romo retired, 'now I bleed green'
jokes.setup: Charlie calls Mac out for being a Cowboys fan at an Eagles Super Bowl
jokes.punchline: Mac's allegiance isn't to a team at all — it's to a single player, and he's seamlessly transferred his loyalty to the Eagles now that Romo is gone
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific logic — Mac applies his own idiosyncratic rules to fandom that make a twisted kind of sense. The confidence with which he delivers it sells it. Slightly undermined by being a quick bit in a busy scene.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm not a Cowboy fan, I'm a Tony Romo fan, and he retired, so now I bleed green.

jokes.text: Mac notices something wrong with Dee's eye; Dee claims she just 'slept on it funny'
jokes.setup: Mac notices Dee's eye is twitching and blinking abnormally
jokes.punchline: Dee's escalating denial ('I slept on it funny') about what is clearly a serious eye infection — the first plant of a running gag
jokes.explanation: The setup of the episode-long running gag. Dee's denial is in character and the visual implied by 'scratching it and it's blinking' is appropriately disgusting. Gets a rewatch bonus because on second viewing you're tracking how early the infection appears.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What's going on with your eye?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Nothing, I got a... I think I got an eyelash in it. You're, like, scratching it and it's blinking... I just, I slept on it funny.

jokes.text: Frank's group is chugging beers at 9am before the Super Bowl trip, counting to 15, and immediately trying to post it
jokes.setup: Dennis wants to show the world Philadelphia is not 'just degenerates'
jokes.punchline: Cut to Frank's handpicked guests chugging beers competitively and filming it for social media at 9am
jokes.explanation: Good juxtaposition joke — Dennis's speech about dignity immediately undercut by the guests' behavior. The specific detail of counting to 15 (a lot of beers) and posting it elevates it from generic degenerate behavior.

dialogue.line: Chug, chug, chug... That's 15. Post that, Jack, post it, baby.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'You have literally picked out the biggest pieces of shit in the city.' Frank: 'I got to agree with that. These guys are pieces of shit.'
jokes.setup: Dennis accuses Frank of picking the worst possible people to represent Philadelphia
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately agrees — he has zero defensiveness about having chosen terrible people
jokes.explanation: Frank's total lack of shame is perfectly in character. The rhythm of Dennis's accusation followed by Frank's chipper agreement is well-executed. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: No big, giant, ridiculous hands.

dialogue.speaker: Fan
dialogue.line: What? What? D-Don't make me go without them.

jokes.text: One of Frank's guests has chewing tobacco in his mouth — 'What is in your mouth?' / 'Chew.' / 'Awesome, cool, good to see you.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is horrified by the caliber of guests Frank has invited
jokes.punchline: Dennis's defeated 'Awesome, cool, good to see you' — the total surrender of a man who has given up
jokes.explanation: Dennis's resigned politeness in the face of genuine grossness is funny precisely because it's so deflated. 'Awesome, cool, good to see you' is a recognizable social script deployed in a completely inappropriate context.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You have literally picked out the biggest pieces of shit in the city.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I got to agree with that. These guys are pieces of shit.

jokes.text: Cricket arrives with a bleeding nose, explaining: 'I came up portside on a horse, and he was a little quicker than me... that's lesson learned.'
jokes.setup: Cricket shows up and his nose is bleeding; Dennis asks why
jokes.punchline: Cricket's nonchalant explanation that he tried to race a horse and lost, delivered as a minor inconvenience rather than the horrifying event it is
jokes.explanation: Cricket's ongoing physical deterioration is a series-long dark joke, and 'I came up portside on a horse' as a casual explanation for a bleeding nose is perfectly on-brand. The specificity of 'portside' (a nautical term applied to a horse race) adds absurdist texture. 'That's lesson learned' as the entire takeaway from being beaten by a horse is excellent character comedy. High character integration score because ONLY Cricket's arc makes this work.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What is in your mouth?

dialogue.speaker: Fan
dialogue.line: Chew.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Awesome, cool, good to see you.

jokes.text: Dennis's 'alternate' to Cricket turns out to be Rex — a blandly positive guy in a polo shirt — presented as the peak of Philadelphia civilization
jokes.setup: Dennis kicks Cricket out for being the worst representation of the city and announces he has an 'alternate'
jokes.punchline: Rex is comically normal compared to the gang, making him seem like a paragon — but he immediately starts pitching his pyramid scheme
jokes.explanation: The setup works — Rex seems like a relief after Cricket — but the payoff (he's also terrible, just differently terrible) takes a while to land. Decent slow-burn character introduction.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Your nose is bleeding as we speak.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Okay, I came up portside on a horse, and he was a little quicker than me... that's lesson learned.

jokes.text: Frank's surprise reveal: the bus has a fully stocked bar
jokes.setup: Frank teases a 'last surprise' as everyone boards the party bus
jokes.punchline: The surprise is a bar — which the degenerate crowd treats as a genuine delight, completely normalizing it
jokes.explanation: Functional gag that fits the show's ethos. Not particularly clever, but lands adequately as a payoff to Frank's tease.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Rex represents the best that Philadelphia has to offer.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Either way, Cricks, you're out.

jokes.text: Charlie finds his Green Man suit at the last second, everyone celebrates, then immediately: 'Can we go now?'
jokes.setup: Charlie has been desperately searching for his Green Man suit, the gang is anxious to leave
jokes.punchline: The 'triumph' of finding the suit is immediately deflated by the mundane impatience of 'can we go now?' — the emotional climax is punctured instantly
jokes.explanation: Good comic structure — brief false climax immediately undercut. The 'can we go now?' lands because it acknowledges the absurdity of celebrating finding a costume. Economical beat.

dialogue.line: Is this a bar?
Nice. Nice.
Fully stocked, baby.

jokes.text: The gang is singing the Eagles fight song for the tenth time on the bus because 'it turns out there's not that many songs about Philadelphia'
jokes.setup: Everyone groans as the Eagles chant starts AGAIN
jokes.punchline: Charlie's sheepish admission that there's just not a lot of Philadelphia-specific song material — delivered as if this is a reasonable explanation for the repetition
jokes.explanation: Self-aware gag that works because it's true (Philadelphia songs are limited) and because Charlie's obliviousness to why the tenth repetition is annoying is in character. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: L. E. S. Eagles.

jokes.text: Cricket has disguised himself as Charlie and snuck onto the bus; his nose gives him away
jokes.setup: Mac notices someone bleeding and asks what happened to 'Charlie's' nose
jokes.punchline: It's Cricket in disguise — his perpetually bleeding nose being his tell is a perfect Cricket-specific detail
jokes.explanation: The reveal works because Cricket's bleeding nose is both a callback to the earlier horse joke and a character-specific tell that couldn't belong to anyone else. The willingness to try the disguise despite the obvious bleed-through shows Cricket's particular brand of desperate optimism. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Fan
dialogue.line: This is, like, the tenth time.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, i-it turns out there's not that many songs about Philadelphia.

jokes.text: Mac deliberates about going back for Charlie: 'I don't want to set a precedent of little mishaps setting us back'
jokes.setup: They've left Charlie behind and are debating whether to turn around
jokes.punchline: Mac frames leaving a friend behind as a 'little mishap' and his main concern is about precedent-setting rather than Charlie's welfare
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny selfishness framed as reasonable policy-making. 'Setting a precedent' is the wrong register for this situation, and Mac's managerial tone about abandoning Charlie is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: All right, fine, it's me. Cricket.
Cricket.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Yes, it's me, it's me. I snuck on, all right? This damn nose.

jokes.text: Mac reinstates Cricket ('Cricket, you're back in') immediately after kicking him out, with zero acknowledgment of the reversal
jokes.setup: Mac was firm that Cricket represented the worst of Philadelphia and had to go
jokes.punchline: Now that the alternative is turning the bus around, Cricket is instantly rehabilitated with no explanation
jokes.explanation: The hypocrisy is in-character for the gang, and the speed of the reversal is the joke. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't want to set a precedent of little mishaps setting us back, so... Cricket, you're back in.

jokes.text: The Waitress doesn't like football. Mac's response: 'She don't even like football.' Then: 'I'm not missing a second of my dreamboat, Tommy Terrific.'
jokes.setup: Mac wants to leave the Waitress behind since Charlie isn't turning around for her
jokes.punchline: The Waitress reveals she's there entirely to see Tom Brady, not for football at all — she's the mirror of the gang's superstition absurdity but applied to celebrity crush
jokes.explanation: 'Tommy Terrific' is a good touch. The Waitress's obsession with Brady as a dreamboat while hating football is a funny inversion — she's as irrational as the gang, just with different motivation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Sh-She don't even like football.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Yeah, football sucks. But if Charlie missed the bus, he missed the bus. I'm not missing a second of my dreamboat, Tommy Terrific.

jokes.text: The Waitress chants 'Go, Pats' while literally on a Philadelphia Eagles party bus, surrounded by Eagles fans
jokes.setup: The bus full of Eagles fans is heading to the Super Bowl
jokes.punchline: The Waitress cheerfully rooting for the opposing team, in enemy territory, with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Quick physical/character beat. The cringe of her cheerfully yelling for the Pats on a Philly bus is good. The 'shit, pothole' interruption adds nice absurdist punctuation.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Go, Pats. Go, Pats. Go, Pats.

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Drive. Drive. Go, Pats. Go, Pats.

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.line: Shit, pothole.

jokes.text: Something 'kicks loose inside' Frank on the bus after a pothole — the first hint of the kidney stone subplot
jokes.setup: The bus hits a pothole
jokes.punchline: Frank cryptically announces 'Something kicked loose inside' — the horrifying implication played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Perfect plant for the episode's main B-plot. The vagueness of 'something kicked loose inside' is funnier than a direct statement would be, and it rewards rewatch knowing what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You're involved in that pyramid scheme, too? / No. No hocking berries at the Super Bowl, Rex. Just be meat, okay?

dialogue.speaker: Rex
dialogue.line: Well... take off your shirt, please.

jokes.text: Rex pitches 'Invigaron berries' as a supplement on the Super Bowl party bus — 'You're involved in that pyramid scheme, too?'
jokes.setup: Rex offers a 'protein shake' to the ailing Frank
jokes.punchline: The shake reveals Rex is in a berry pyramid scheme — apparently widespread enough that Dennis recognizes it immediately
jokes.explanation: Multilevel marketing parody is familiar territory but the specific deployment here — on a Super Bowl party bus as Rex's introduction — is reasonably well-timed. 'No hocking berries at the Super Bowl, Rex. Just be meat' is a funny line.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No, no, no. They don't have axles there. But I can get a new pair of jean shorts.

jokes.text: Mac instructs Rex: 'No hocking berries at the Super Bowl, Rex. Just be meat, okay? Well... take off your shirt, please.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to control the group's behavior at the Super Bowl
jokes.punchline: 'Just be meat' is an instruction with zero normal meaning, followed by Mac telling a stranger to take his shirt off as if this is a reasonable ask
jokes.explanation: 'Just be meat' is an excellent line — completely meaningless yet somehow communicates exactly what Mac wants (a large, shirtless, impressive physical specimen). The pivot to 'take off your shirt, please' as a normal request is well-executed. High economy score for maximum weirdness in minimum words.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: We invite the wrong crowd, and now we've got people going on expeditions for jean shorts. And hocking magical berries and rooting for the Patriots?

jokes.text: Dee's eye has gotten visibly worse; she responds: 'I get it, I get it. It's Pick on Dee for No Reason Day. Real original.'
jokes.setup: Mac is visibly alarmed by how much worse Dee's eye has gotten
jokes.punchline: Dee interprets a genuine medical concern as typical bullying and dismisses it — her denial is so complete she's framing the symptoms as the gang's invention
jokes.explanation: The running gag escalation is working well here. 'Pick on Dee for No Reason Day' is a great line because it's both obviously false (she clearly has pink eye) and yet also believable as a thing the gang would do. Good character integration — Dee's defensiveness about being the butt of jokes is a core character trait.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well... E-A-G-L-E-S. Eagles.

jokes.text: Mac delivers bad news: the axle is bent and the bus isn't going anywhere — but the good news is there's a Walmart nearby... so Frank can get new jean shorts
jokes.setup: Mac sets up a classic 'good news/bad news' structure about the broken bus
jokes.punchline: The 'good news' is not 'we can get parts' but 'Frank can replace his grease-stained jean shorts at Walmart' — the wrong problem is being solved
jokes.explanation: The good news/bad news structure is set up cleanly then subverted — the 'good news' is useless to the actual problem but perfect to Frank's personal priorities. The specificity of 'jean shorts' as the thing Frank cares about is excellent. Well-structured misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, we made it to the Super Bowl. That was easy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah, it was incredibly smooth.

jokes.text: Dennis's breakdown: 'Every single thing we do turns to shit... we are never, ever gonna make it to the Super Bowl'
jokes.setup: The bus is broken down; Dennis is spiraling about the failed trip
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a sincere, operatic lament — which is funny because (a) it's disproportionate and (b) we know they'll get there
jokes.explanation: Dennis's melodrama is familiar. Works adequately as a character moment but isn't especially novel. Functions more as a structural beat than a true joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Let's-let's cool it on the boos, you know? That's-that's kind of, like, what we're famous for, you know? We-we boo ourselves, we boo the Eagles, we boo Santa Claus.

jokes.text: Immediately after Dennis's 'we'll never make it' speech, cut to: 'Hi, everyone. Welcome to Super Bowl LII.' / 'Well, we made it to the Super Bowl. That was easy.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just declared with total certainty that they will never make it to the Super Bowl
jokes.punchline: Instant cut to them arriving. Mac's 'That was easy' is a deadpan acknowledgment that the entire crisis was skipped over
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural editing joke. The gap between Dennis's despair and the instant arrival is maximally funny, and Mac's self-aware 'that was easy' treats the entire breakdown as beneath comment. The economy is exceptional — the joke lives in the cut, not the dialogue. 'Incredibly smooth' adds an additional layer of unreliable narrator comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We-we boo ourselves, we boo the Eagles, we boo Santa Claus.

jokes.text: Mac instructs the group: 'Let's cool it on the boos... we boo ourselves, we boo the Eagles, we boo Santa Claus.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to coach the group on proper fan behavior at the Super Bowl
jokes.punchline: His list of things Philly fans boo includes their own team and Santa Claus — a real historical reference that lands as absurdist
jokes.explanation: The Santa Claus reference (Eagles fans infamously booed Santa Claus in 1968) is a well-known Philadelphia sports fact, so it functions as both observational comedy and a nod to the audience. 'We boo ourselves' is the unexpected escalation. Good quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Okay, "Everybody look at me, I'm a stupid Pats fan, making up stuff about Dee's eye."

jokes.text: Dee is confronted about her eye: 'Dee, you definitely have pink eye.' Her response: 'I don't have pink... all right. Would a person with pink eye do this?'
jokes.setup: Dee's eye has continued to worsen; someone finally diagnoses it as pink eye
jokes.punchline: Dee challenges the diagnosis by doing something with her eye that presumably looks absolutely horrible — the joke is entirely visual, with the audience seeing what 'this' is
jokes.explanation: The 'would a person with pink eye do THIS?' beat is a classic cringe escalation. The visual of whatever Dee does with her infected eye to prove she doesn't have pink eye is the joke, and it's a strong one. The logic (doing something disgusting with an infected eye somehow disproves the infection) is perfect Dee self-sabotage.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Would a person with pink eye do this?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Would she do that?

jokes.text: Frank has been pushing the call button nonstop and reports: 'I choked down some dogs too fast. They didn't settle, you know? They came back up, actually. On the other dogs.'
jokes.setup: A waiter arrives annoyed that someone has been mashing the call button
jokes.punchline: Frank explains he ate hot dogs too fast and they came back up — but then he continued eating more hot dogs on top of the vomit
jokes.explanation: 'They came back up, actually. On the other dogs.' is a genuinely disgusting and funny escalation. The beat between 'didn't settle' and the clarification builds perfectly. Frank's matter-of-fact delivery of something revolting is high character integration. The 'on the other dogs' specificity is what elevates it above generic gross-out.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I choked down some dogs too fast. They-they didn't settle, you know? They came back up, actually. On the other dogs.

jokes.text: The waiter turns out to be someone the gang has apparently wronged in the past ('How did I move all the way to Minnesota and I'm still waiting on you people?') — but the gang has zero memory of him
jokes.setup: The waiter recognizes the gang with apparent trauma
jokes.punchline: The gang denies any connection and Mac says 'You never waited on us' with total confidence — their damage to others is so extensive they can't track individual victims
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny structural joke about the gang's obliviousness to their own impact. 'How did I move all the way to Minnesota and I'm still waiting on you people?' captures the ongoing horror of anyone adjacent to the gang. 'It's not worth recapping. What's the point?' is the waiter giving up — a great beat. High character integration because the joke only works given how terrible the gang is to service workers throughout the series.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: How did I move all the way to Minnesota, and I'm still waiting on you people?

dialogue.speaker: Gang
dialogue.line: I-I don't know this guy.

dialogue.speaker: Gang
dialogue.line: No, you never waited on us. We don't live in Minnesota, bud.

jokes.text: Rex immediately tries to pitch Invigaron berries to the visibly stressed waiter: 'You're kind of frail. You need to get swole.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to defuse the tension with the angry waiter
jokes.punchline: Rex, reading the room completely wrong, pivots to his pyramid scheme pitch — 'you're kind of frail, you need to get swole' as an opener
jokes.explanation: Rex's total social obliviousness in service of his MLM is consistent character work. 'You need to get swole' as a sales opener is funny in its specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I tied his shoelaces together.

jokes.text: Frank reveals: 'I tied his shoelaces together.'
jokes.setup: The waiter has walked away after declining Rex's pitch
jokes.punchline: Frank casually announces he has sabotaged the waiter who annoyed him — the pettiness of tying shoelaces as revenge is perfectly Frank
jokes.explanation: Five words. Perfectly Frank. The pettiness of a tied-shoelace prank from a grown man who could easily harm someone worse is somehow exactly right for the character — childish malice. Maximum economy (9.5) because the entire joke is four words and a period. High character integration because only Frank would do this as a casual, unannounced act of minor vengeance. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: This Minnesota rube, he's not ready for your big-city shenanigans, Frank.

jokes.text: Mac's reaction to Frank's shoelace sabotage: 'This Minnesota rube, he's not ready for your big-city shenanigans, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank announces he tied the waiter's shoelaces together
jokes.punchline: Mac responds as if tying shoelaces together is sophisticated 'big-city shenanigans' that a simple Minnesota man couldn't be expected to anticipate
jokes.explanation: Mac's framing of a kindergarten prank as 'big-city shenanigans' that only an urban sophisticate would employ is a great ironic inversion. It also implies Mac thinks Philadelphia is a cosmopolitan city of refined trickery, which plays into the show's self-aggrandizing delusion theme.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I felt a little piece of kidney stone break off and go through the, into the bladder.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why didn't you tell me that you have a kidney stone, dude?

jokes.text: Frank reveals he has a kidney stone — 'I felt a little piece of kidney stone break off and go through, into the bladder' — announced casually on a party bus
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank are in the bathroom and Frank seems unwell
jokes.punchline: Frank has been suffering from a kidney stone since the bus ride and kept it secret to avoid 'freaking anyone out'
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the pothole setup. The clinical description of the kidney stone fragment's journey ('broke off and go through, into the bladder') delivered matter-of-factly is good. Frank's reason for hiding it — 'I don't want to freak you out' — is characteristically bizarre given that he's now freaking everyone out more.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You can't see because you have a very serious bacterial infection in your eye.

jokes.text: Mac's response to the kidney stone: 'This kidney stone better not screw us up.' Then Frank: 'I can manage. This ain't my first rodeo.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just revealed he has a painful kidney stone
jokes.punchline: Mac's concern is entirely about the game, not Frank's health. Frank's 'this ain't my first rodeo' implies he has had kidney stones before and considers them routine
jokes.explanation: 'This ain't my first rodeo' applied to kidney stones is a great use of a cliché in the wrong context. Mac's callousness about Frank's pain is on-brand. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Ding-dong here's getting honored with the rest of the vets. I'm gonna sneak down there with him. When we get close to the field, I'm gonna let you in on a little plan I've whipped up.

jokes.text: Frank: 'This ain't my first rodeo.' — said about managing a kidney stone, immediately followed by missing the Eagles touchdown.
jokes.setup: Mac is worried Frank's kidney stone will cause them to miss key game moments
jokes.punchline: Frank's confident 'ain't my first rodeo' (implying he's experienced with kidney stones) is immediately contradicted — they miss the touchdown while he's managing the stone
jokes.explanation: The 'ain't my first rodeo' brag being immediately proved wrong is a good structural beat. Frank having multiple prior kidney stone experiences is dark and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So, you know what, you can go, but I'm, I'm just gonna cover you up so people don't know that you're from Philadelphia.

jokes.text: Dee on the view from their terrible seats: 'Who knows? I can't see a goddamn thing this high up. These seats are the worst.' / 'You can't see because you have a very serious bacterial infection in your eye.'
jokes.setup: Nobody saw the Eagles' touchdown because they were away; Dee is asked how they scored
jokes.punchline: Dee blames the seats; Mac correctly identifies that her pink eye has progressed to a 'serious bacterial infection'
jokes.explanation: Good running gag escalation — 'pink eye' has now become 'serious bacterial infection.' The dual explanation (bad seats / bad eye) compounds the joke. Dee's continued denial tracks perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Luxury suite? Napkins? Utensils? We're going soft up here in this ivory tower.

jokes.text: Mac notices Cricket has new hands: 'Hey, you got new hands.' Cricket: 'Yeah. I like them.'
jokes.setup: Mac notices something different about Cricket mid-scene
jokes.punchline: Cricket has obtained entirely new prosthetic or replacement hands — treated with the same casual acceptance as a new haircut. Cricket's simple 'I like them' is the entire character.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Cricket's ongoing physical destruction is a series-long dark joke, but the casual nonchalance of 'you got new hands' / 'yeah, I like them' is a masterclass in economy and character integration. No explanation is given for why he needed new hands or where he got them. The refusal to explain is the joke. 'I like them' as Cricket's entire emotional response to apparently having his hands replaced is devastating and hilarious. Near-perfect character integration score because this only works in the context of Cricket's entire series arc.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Tom Brady does not care that you are here.

jokes.text: Mac covers Dee's face with something to hide her pink eye 'so people don't know you're from Philadelphia'
jokes.setup: Dee wants to accompany Cricket to sneak down toward the field
jokes.punchline: Mac's solution to Dee's grotesque infected eyes is to cover her face — framed as a PR concern for Philadelphia rather than concern for Dee
jokes.explanation: The framing of 'so people don't know you're from Philadelphia' is a good twist — it's not about helping Dee, it's about image management. Fits neatly into the episode's Philadelphia reputation theme.

dialogue.speaker: Rex
dialogue.line: It's the Invigoron berries, man. They're loaded with sugar, but I'm in too deep. I've got to sell 40 cases of this stuff or I'm gonna lose my apartment.

jokes.text: Mac to the gang wanting to leave the box: 'Tom Brady does not care that you are here.'
jokes.setup: The Waitress implies her presence at the Super Bowl should matter to Tom Brady
jokes.punchline: Mac's flat, accurate dismissal of the Waitress's delusion — Tom Brady is unaware she exists
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the flat truth delivered without elaboration. Mac being the voice of reason about someone else's delusion while having his own (the superstitions, the fan impact) is an ironic double that adds depth.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Hell yeah, another Patriots touchdown. Tommy Touchdown coming to get y'all. Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You know what? You get out, too.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: I can go?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: All right. Tommy, Mama's coming.

jokes.text: Rex explains why he can't take his shirt off: 'It's the Invigaron berries, man. They're loaded with sugar, but I'm in too deep. I've got to sell 40 cases of this stuff or I'm gonna lose my apartment.'
jokes.setup: Mac has repeatedly asked Rex to take his shirt off to 'just be meat'; Rex won't
jokes.punchline: Rex has been consuming his own pyramid scheme product compulsively despite knowing it's just sugar, and is now physically distended, unable to meet his quota, and about to lose housing
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Rex is consuming his own MLM product and is now physically compromised by it is a good escalation. 'I'm in too deep' applied to berry consumption is funny. The specificity of 40 cases and losing his apartment gives it stakes that make it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Every time Frank goes to the bathroom, the Eagles score.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you pissing?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Piss, Frank, piss.

jokes.text: The Waitress celebrates a Patriots touchdown: 'Hell yeah, another Patriots touchdown. Tommy Touchdown coming to get y'all. Yes.'
jokes.setup: The Patriots score; Eagles fans are upset
jokes.punchline: The Waitress celebrates enthusiastically in the Eagles luxury box, calling Brady 'Tommy Touchdown'
jokes.explanation: Consistent character work. 'Tommy Touchdown' is a fun nickname. The cringe of celebrating in enemy territory is maintained well.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm pissing, and it hurts like shit.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Just keep peeing. I don't know. It's not updating.

jokes.text: Mac kicks the Waitress out of the box for cheering the Patriots — 'You know what? You get out, too.' 'I can go? All right. Tommy, Mama's coming.'
jokes.setup: Mac is annoyed by the Waitress's Patriots enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: The Waitress is thrilled to be ejected because it means she can go find Brady — 'Tommy, Mama's coming' is simultaneously delusional and terrifying
jokes.explanation: 'Tommy, Mama's coming' is a great line — it has the energy of a threat disguised as affection. The Waitress turning punishment into opportunity is consistent with her character's tunnel vision. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Frank, drink.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Got to piss.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I need you to piss through this entire game, Frank. We can't leave this bathroom. The Eagles need us.

jokes.text: Every time Frank goes to the bathroom, the Eagles score — Mac discovers this pattern and declares Frank must stay in the bathroom
jokes.setup: Frank needs to urinate because of his kidney stone; Mac has taken him to the bathroom multiple times and each time the Eagles have scored
jokes.punchline: Mac applies the same superstition logic to Frank's urination as Charlie applies to the Green Man suit — Frank's painful kidney stone passage is now a sacred ritual
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — Mac, who explicitly mocked Charlie's superstitions at the top of the episode, has now become a full superstition convert and is forcing Frank to urinate in pain for the Eagles. The hypocritical reversal is well-earned. 'Piss, Frank, piss' as Mac's new battle cry is a great line. Rewatch bonus for catching the hypocrisy callback.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Perfect timing, man. I need to get this out to Brady. Brady's ready to go out. He's really wiping that sweat off with that towel. I mean, he's really going at it.

jokes.text: Mac coaching Frank through painful kidney stone urination: 'I'm pissing, and it hurts like shit.' / Mac: 'Just keep peeing. I don't know. It's not updating.'
jokes.setup: Frank is painfully urinating in a Super Bowl bathroom while Mac monitors the game score on his phone
jokes.punchline: 'It's not updating' — Mac treating the game score app as a toilet coaching tool, frustrated by poor wifi in a stadium bathroom during a Super Bowl
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Frank's genuine pain ('it hurts like shit') against Mac's mundane technology frustration ('it's not updating') is a perfect tonal collision. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I can't piss no more. It hurts like shit.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You got to force it out, then.

jokes.text: Mac instructs Pondy to bring as much beer to the bathroom as possible so Frank can keep urinating, declaring: 'The Eagles need us.'
jokes.setup: An Eagles score has been attributed to Frank's urination; Mac wants to maintain the stream
jokes.punchline: Mac is now running a beer-to-bathroom pipeline to keep Frank urinating indefinitely, framed as a patriotic duty to the Eagles
jokes.explanation: 'The Eagles need us' as the justification for forcing beer into an ill man to maintain a painful urination stream is a great absurdist escalation. The gravity Mac brings to it is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Rex
dialogue.line: It's a berry found deep in the jungles of the Amazon forest, and available for the first time. I'm a happy client.

jokes.text: Security stops someone and demands a pass — visual/reaction beat as Cricket and Dee apparently try to bluff their way past security
jokes.setup: Cricket and Dee have snuck down toward the field
jokes.punchline: Security confronts them — Dee's grotesque eye and Cricket's general appearance presumably making them extremely conspicuous
jokes.explanation: Limited comedy value from the transcript alone — this is primarily a visual/setup beat for what comes next. The inference that security stopping Cricket and infected-eye Dee is funny is reasonable but under-realized in the dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We are Philadelphia. These guys are a total embarrassment. We blew it, man.

jokes.text: On the field: 'Open your eyes.' / Dee: 'Sorry...' — Dee apparently can't see and is bumping into people on the field
jokes.setup: Dee has made it to the field level but her eye infection has progressed to near-blindness
jokes.punchline: She's stumbling around near the Super Bowl field, bumping into people, with a catastrophically infected eye
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff in an unexpected location. Dee staggering around the Super Bowl field half-blind is absurd and fitting. Primarily a visual gag so the transcript undersells it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Because that's who he is, man. And you know who we are? We're losers. All of Philadelphia. We're angry, and we're mean and we're cruel.

jokes.text: On the sideline: 'I need to get this out to Brady.' / 'Brady's ready to go out. He's really wiping that sweat off with that towel.'
jokes.setup: Cricket has apparently gotten near the Patriots sideline with some kind of substance
jokes.punchline: The implication that Cricket is trying to deliver something (Dee's pink eye discharge?) to Brady — framed with the mundane detail of Brady wiping his face with a towel
jokes.explanation: The implication that Cricket is transmitting Dee's pink eye infection to Tom Brady through a towel (or similar) is a brilliantly dark long-game payoff. The transcript is coy about it ('squirt some out, man') but the implication is clear and disgusting. The sportscaster-style observation 'he's really wiping that sweat off with that towel' makes the horror mundane and therefore funnier. Strong rewatch bonus for seeing how early the setup begins.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No. Those guys, those guys are Philadelphia. They bust their ass every day just to get through.

jokes.text: 'I can't piss no more. It hurts like shit.' / Mac: 'You got to force it out, then.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been urinating in the bathroom for an extended period in extreme pain
jokes.punchline: Frank's kidney stone has apparently stopped the flow; Mac's coaching response is to tell him to push harder
jokes.explanation: The bathroom sequence continues to escalate. Mac as an unsympathetic kidney stone coach ('force it out, then') is appropriately callous. Functional escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Those guys, those guys are Philadelphia. They bust their ass every day just to get through. And then, on a Sunday, they put all their hopes into the Eagles.

jokes.text: Mac instructs a random off-duty waiter in the bathroom: 'You, you. Ten beers, stat.' Waiter: 'I'm off duty, just here to go to the bathroom.'
jokes.setup: Mac needs more beer to keep Frank urinating
jokes.punchline: Mac tries to conscript a random bathroom-goer as wait staff — the man is simply trying to use the bathroom in peace at the Super Bowl
jokes.explanation: 'Ten beers, stat' as a bathroom command is good. The ordinary man's ordinary response ('I'm off duty, just here to go to the bathroom') creates a perfect mundane/absurd collision.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: And they get angry. And that anger builds into a stone of fury. And if it could just be released, then we could feel something different.

jokes.text: Rex pitches Invigaron to a stranger on the field, claiming to be 'a happy client'
jokes.setup: Rex has somehow made it out of the box and is on the field
jokes.punchline: His priority in this once-in-a-lifetime field access is to sell pyramid scheme berries — he's also apparently now selling to himself
jokes.explanation: Consistent character beat. Rex's compulsive selling at inappropriate moments is his defining trait. Diminishing returns on the berry joke at this point, but 'I'm a happy client' is a funny MLM-speak detail.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: And that anger builds into a stone of fury. And if it could just be released, then we could feel something different.

jokes.text: News broadcast: 'And it's always nice to see our nation's troops being honored.' Cut to the gang's degenerates having apparently blundered into the veteran's ceremony on the field
jokes.setup: The Super Bowl halftime/ceremony involves honoring veterans
jokes.punchline: The Philadelphia degenerates have somehow infiltrated the ceremony and are being shown on national television as if they are veterans
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of the sincere tribute announcement with the visual of the gang's degenerates being honored is a good dark irony gag. The earnest announcer line makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do it for the Birds, Frank. Do it for the whole city of Philadelphia, man, push.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: Brady, with White to his right, takes the snap.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do it like Rocky, man. Push.

jokes.text: Dennis watching the gang on TV at the ceremony: 'We are Philadelphia. These guys are a total embarrassment.'
jokes.setup: Dennis watches in horror as his group humiliates Philadelphia on national television
jokes.punchline: His verdict — 'total embarrassment' — is delivered with the gravity of someone who considers himself the standard of non-embarrassment, despite being a member of the same group
jokes.explanation: Dennis's total lack of self-awareness about his own role in the embarrassment is classic. 'We are Philadelphia' as a proud declaration immediately followed by 'total embarrassment' is a good self-undermining rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do it like Rocky, man. Push.

jokes.text: Mac's breakdown in the bathroom: 'You know who we are? We're losers. All of Philadelphia. We're angry, and we're mean and we're cruel. And we act like jerks...'
jokes.setup: Brady has the ball with 2.5 minutes left and Mac is spiraling
jokes.punchline: Mac's sincere self-diagnosis of Philadelphia (and the gang) as fundamentally broken people — delivered as a revelation, but it's just an accurate description of the show's premise
jokes.explanation: Meta joke about the show's own premise — the gang describing themselves accurately is funny. 'We're angry, and mean and cruel' as a self-aware confession has some pathos that elevates it slightly above pure comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: Brady lost the ball. Looks like he couldn't see the defender. It's-it's like something was wrong with his eyes.

jokes.text: Frank's speech about Philadelphia: 'That anger builds into a stone of fury'
jokes.setup: Frank is delivering an impassioned speech about the soul of Philadelphia fans
jokes.punchline: 'A stone of fury' — Frank's kidney stone metaphor accidentally (or deliberately) describes his literal medical condition as a spiritual truth about the city
jokes.explanation: The best single line in the episode. Frank delivering an earnest speech about Philadelphia's collective anger culminating in 'a stone of fury' is a perfect double-meaning — he's simultaneously describing Philadelphia fans and his own kidney stone, without apparently being aware of the connection. The fact that his speech then pivots to 'you've got to push that stone out right now' makes the metaphor literal. High earned-vs-cheap and character integration because only Frank could deliver this speech in this context.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You did it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No, Mac. We did it. We did it. We did it.

jokes.text: Mac coaching Frank to pass his kidney stone like Rocky: 'Do it like Rocky, man. Push.'
jokes.setup: Frank needs to pass his kidney stone while Mac provides motivational coaching
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes Rocky — the ultimate Philadelphia sports motivation — in the context of forcing urine through a kidney stone in a stadium bathroom
jokes.explanation: Rocky as the patron saint of kidney stone passage is a perfect Philadelphia gag. The image of Mac doing a Rocky-style pep talk in a stadium bathroom is vivid and funny. Good economy, high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't know why you care, fair-weather fan.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Fair-weather fan. You're from Minnesota, that's okay.

jokes.text: News broadcast: 'Brady lost the ball. Looks like he couldn't see the defender. It's-it's like something was wrong with his eyes.'
jokes.setup: Brady fumbles the ball; the announcer tries to explain what happened
jokes.punchline: The announcer notes Brady seemed to have trouble with his eyes — confirming that Cricket successfully transmitted Dee's pink eye to Tom Brady during the game
jokes.explanation: The long-game payoff of the entire episode's B-plot. Dee's pink eye, introduced in the first 40 seconds, has been transmitted to Tom Brady via Cricket's sideline infiltration, causing the fumble that wins the Eagles the Super Bowl. The announcer's clinical bewilderment ('it's like something was wrong with his eyes') is the perfect deadpan confirmation. This is the strongest structural joke in the episode — a 15-minute setup paid off in one line delivered by an oblivious third party. The show literally rewrites the Super Bowl LII narrative (which the Eagles actually won) around a pink eye conspiracy. Exceptional craft.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: I'm over Tommy Fumbles. I'm all about my man, Nick Foles.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Gross.

jokes.text: 'You did it.' / Frank: 'No, Mac. We did it.'
jokes.setup: The Eagles have won and Mac credits Frank's kidney stone urination
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'we did it' — meaning he and Mac's collective bathroom heroism — is treated with total sincerity, as if they genuinely won the Super Bowl for Philadelphia from a stadium bathroom
jokes.explanation: The earnest team-building moment in a stadium bathroom is a good parody of sports movies. 'No, Mac. We did it' as a profound statement about two men who just shared a kidney stone experience is appropriately absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What did you do?. You sons of bitches, this is your fault. You screwed it up.

jokes.text: Mac to the waiter: 'I don't know why you care, fair-weather fan. Fair-weather fan. You're from Minnesota, that's okay.'
jokes.setup: The waiter is celebrating or reacting to the Eagles win
jokes.punchline: Mac dismisses the waiter's reaction by calling him a 'fair-weather fan' — despite the waiter presumably not being an Eagles fan at all, and Mac himself being a Cowboys fan until very recently
jokes.explanation: Mac calling someone else a fair-weather fan when he was literally a Cowboys fan three hours ago is perfect hypocrisy. The 'You're from Minnesota, that's okay' condescension is a nice tag.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do a superstition. Frank. Pee. Pee. Pee.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm dry.

jokes.text: The Waitress, immediately after celebrating the Eagles' win, declares: 'I'm over Tommy Fumbles. I'm all about my man, Nick Foles.'
jokes.setup: The Eagles win; Brady has fumbled and lost
jokes.punchline: The Waitress has instantly abandoned her Brady obsession and transferred her romantic fixation to Eagles QB Nick Foles — 'Tommy Fumbles' as an instant nickname for the man she called 'Tommy Terrific' minutes ago
jokes.explanation: 'Tommy Fumbles' as the instant rebrand of 'Tommy Terrific' is an excellent callback. The speed with which she transfers obsessive attachment from one quarterback to another reveals that it was never about Brady — it's a pattern. 'Gross' as the gang's reaction is perfect. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, you're gonna have to get back in that trap.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Aw, come on, man. You just told me to get out of it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, that was before Brady had the ball.

jokes.text: Dennis's apology speech is immediately interrupted: 'Wait, wait, wait. Brady got the ball back, and there's 58 seconds left in the game.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered a sincere apology and declared they helped the Eagles win the Super Bowl
jokes.punchline: The game isn't over — the entire victory celebration and apology tour was premature, and Brady still has the ball
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom false resolution — the moment they think they've won, the stakes return. Well-timed deflation of Dennis's sincere moment. 'You sons of bitches, this is your fault' is a good immediate reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You just told me to get out of it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, that was before Brady had the ball.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Does it have to be the same leg or...

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Same leg.

jokes.text: 'You sons of bitches, this is your fault. You screwed it up.'
jokes.setup: Brady still has the ball after the gang's premature celebration
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately blames the gang — specifically for celebrating too early, as if the celebration itself caused Brady to get the ball back
jokes.explanation: Mac's immediate pivot from celebration to blame is consistent with his character. The superstition logic (celebrating too early = cursed it) is consistent with the episode's theme. Quick and functional.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: He's hit. He stumbles.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do it, do it now.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: He's throwing. He is going deep for the end zone, and it is... batted around... and incomplete. And the game is over.

jokes.text: Mac instructs someone to do a superstition 'quick.' Charlie is called: 'What happened to you?' — Charlie has apparently suffered severe injuries during the episode
jokes.setup: The gang needs to perform superstitions immediately with 58 seconds left
jokes.punchline: Charlie, who was left behind at the beginning, has somehow acquired significant injuries over the course of the episode — the sight gag of his condition is the joke
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Charlie has had an entire parallel adventure and is now injured is a good structural gag. 'It's a long story' and Mac's immediate pivot ('Well, did you do your superstitions?') with zero concern for Charlie's injuries is classic callousness.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We did it. The superstitions are real.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Charlie, you did it. You did it, you were right. The superstitions were real. You did it, man.

jokes.text: Mac instructs Charlie to repeat his exact superstition: 'Does it have to be the same leg?' / 'Same leg.' / 'Damn it.'
jokes.setup: Charlie needs to perform whatever physical superstition he has, but apparently it involves a specific leg
jokes.punchline: The logistics of the superstition involve leg-specific rules, and Charlie's 'Damn it' implies the required leg is injured from his adventure
jokes.explanation: The superstition having a 'same leg' rule is a great absurdist detail — it implies a whole mythology has built up around this ritual that neither Mac nor the audience knows. 'Damn it' as the punchline (the wrong leg is injured) is well-constructed. High economy.

jokes.text: 'We did it. The superstitions are real.'
jokes.setup: Brady's final pass is incomplete; the Eagles win
jokes.punchline: The gang genuinely believes their superstitions (and kidney stone passage) won the Super Bowl — the show's final stance is that they're right
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the episode's main plot — the show commits fully to the absurdist premise that the gang's superstitions (including infecting Brady with pink eye via Cricket) genuinely won the Super Bowl. 'The superstitions are real' as a victorious declaration is a good closing beat.

jokes.text: Mac: 'We did it. We did it. The superstitions are real.' Then: 'Charlie, you did it. You did it, you were right. The superstitions were real. You did it, man.'
jokes.setup: The game ends; the Eagles win
jokes.punchline: Mac's complete, sincere conviction that the superstitions — kidney stone bathroom sessions, leg traps, Green Man suits — won the Super Bowl is the final expression of the episode's central comic premise, delivered with total earnestness
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to the episode's thesis. The comedy comes from Mac's absolute certainty and Charlie's vindication — the show doesn't wink at the audience, it just lets these people believe they won the Super Bowl with magic. This is Sunny's specific brand of dark optimism: terrible people doing terrible things, but they get to feel like winners. The character integration is high because Mac's superstition conversion arc is complete here.

jokes.text: News broadcast: 'It is still a mystery as to what happened with Brady's eye, but it had to have an effect on his play late in the game.'
jokes.setup: Post-game news coverage wraps up the Super Bowl
jokes.punchline: The announcer treats the Brady eye mystery as a genuine sports mystery — the audience knows it's Dee's bacterial pink eye infection, delivered by Cricket
jokes.explanation: The final confirmation of the pink eye conspiracy. The sportscaster framing it as a genuine mystery ('it is still a mystery as to what happened with Brady's eye') while the audience has the full picture is a perfect ironic close. The deadpan authority of the news broadcast selling the premise without winking is excellent structure. Strong earned-vs-cheap because the entire episode builds to this.

jokes.text: Final minute: the gang celebrating in pure, wordless joy. 'They did it. They did it. They did it. They did it.' 'It's over.' 'My God. They did it.'
jokes.setup: The gang celebrates winning — which they interpret as their own victory
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'they did it' is funny because 'they' is both the Eagles AND the Gang in their own minds — these people genuinely believe they caused this Super Bowl win
jokes.explanation: A warm ending beat that works because the show earns its sentiment — these horrible people genuinely bonded over something, even if that something is kidney stones and pink eye. The repeated 'they did it' captures the show's affection for its characters despite everything.

tmdb_overview: It’s the most important weekend of their lives and Frank has treated the gang and a crew of their ragtag hangers-on with tickets to see the Eagles in the Super Bowl!
